**Hydrogen – A Quick Reference to Its Key Properties**

| Category | Property | Typical Value / Description |
|----------|----------|-----------------------------|
| **Basic Identity** | Symbol | H |
| | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | ¹H (protium), ²H (deuterium), ³H (tritium) |
| | State at STP | Gas (colorless, odorless, tasteless) |
| | Boiling point | –252.9 °C (−423.2 °F) |
| | Melting point | –259.2 °C (−434.6 °F) |
| | Density (gas, 0 °C, 1 atm) | 0.0899 g L⁻¹ |
| | Molar volume (ideal gas) | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| | Ionization energy | 13.598 eV |
| | Electron affinity | 0.754 eV |
| | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | First ionization energy | 13.598 eV |
| | Second ionization energy | 27.211 eV |
| | Heat of formation (gas) | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ (by definition) |
| | Standard enthalpy of combustion | –285.83 kJ mol⁻¹ (to H₂O) |
| | Standard Gibbs free energy of formation | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ (by definition) |
| | Standard entropy (gas) | 130.68 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Heat capacity (gas, 25 °C) | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Speed of sound in H₂ | ~1270 m s⁻¹ (at 20 °C) |
| | Refractive index (visible) | ~1.000132 |
| | Viscosity (gas, 25 °C) | 8.76 × 10⁻⁶ Pa·s |
| | Thermal conductivity (gas, 25 °C) | 0.180 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Magnetic susceptibility | Diamagnetic (–2.7 × 10⁻⁶ cm³ mol⁻¹) |
| | Solubility in water | ~1.6 g L⁻¹ at 20 °C |
| | Solubility in ethanol | ~5.5 g L⁻¹ at 20 °C |
| | Solubility in liquid hydrocarbons | ~10–20 g L⁻¹ (varies) |
| | Boiling point of liquid H₂ | –252.9 °C |
| | Critical temperature | –240.4 °C |
| | Critical pressure | 12.8 bar |
| | Critical density | 0.07 g cm⁻³ |
| | Vapor pressure (at 20 °C) | ~0.0001 bar |
| | Dipole moment | 0 D (non‑polar) |
| | Rotational constant (H₂) | 60.853 cm⁻¹ |
| | Vibrational frequency (H₂) | 4401 cm⁻¹ |
| | Bond dissociation energy (H–H) | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Spectral lines | Lyman, Balmer, Paschen series (hydrogen atom); rotational/vibrational bands (H₂) |
| | Nuclear spin | ½ (protium), 1 (deuterium), ½ (tritium) |
| | Magnetic moment | 2.7928 µ_N (protium) |
| | Half‑life (tritium) | 12.32 years |
| | Radioactivity | Tritium is β⁻ emitter (β‑decay to ³He) |
| | Common compounds | H₂O, H₂SO₄, HCl, NH₃, CH₄, etc. |
| | Role in biology | Essential for amino acids, nucleic acids, energy metabolism (ATP) |
| | Role in industry | Fuel (hydrogen fuel cells), ammonia synthesis (Haber–Bosch), petroleum refining, metal hydrides, etc. |
| | Environmental impact | Clean combustion (water vapor); potential for hydrogen economy; storage challenges (low density, high pressure or cryogenic). |
| | Safety | Highly flammable; explosive limits 4–75 % (v/v) in air; requires careful handling. |
| | Isotopic applications | Deuterium used in nuclear fusion research (D–T fusion), neutron sources; tritium used in radiolabeling, fusion experiments. |
| | Quantum properties | Exhibits quantum tunneling in hydrogen bonds; zero‑point energy significant in light‑atom systems. |
| | Spectroscopic constants | Rydberg constant for hydrogen atom: 10973731.5685 cm⁻¹. |
| | Chemical reactivity | Forms covalent bonds with electronegative atoms; forms hydrides (e.g., LiH, NaH). |
| | Oxidation states | +1 (most common), –1 (hydride), 0 (H₂). |
| | Acid–base behavior | Acts as a weak acid (pKa ≈ 35 for H₂O/H₂) and weak base (pKb ≈ 35 for H₂/H₂⁺). |
| | Thermodynamic data | Standard molar enthalpy of formation of H₂(g) = 0; of H₂O(l) = –285.83 kJ mol⁻¹. |
| | Physical constants | Avogadro’s number: 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹; Planck constant: 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s; speed of light: 2.998 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. |

---

### Quick Highlights

- **Lightest element**: Only one proton (and usually one electron).
- **Most abundant**: Makes up ~75 % of the observable universe by mass.
- **Non‑polar**: No permanent dipole moment in its diatomic form.
- **Highly reactive**: Combines with almost all elements; forms a wide variety of compounds.
- **Energy carrier**: Clean combustion produces only water; central to proposed hydrogen economy.
- **Isotopic diversity**: Protium (stable), deuterium (stable, heavier), tritium (radioactive, used in fusion).
- **Quantum significance**: Light mass leads to pronounced quantum effects (zero‑point energy, tunneling).

Feel free to ask for deeper details on any specific property (e.g., spectroscopic data, thermodynamic tables, industrial processes, or isotopic behavior)!
